The finding is valid, and a worker is fixing it on the same branch for change #181 (PR #384). I haven't seen its results yet.

**Cause.** The earlier boolean fix leaves a union with a boolean member as a raw type name, such as `"a|b" | true`. Storybook's converter splits that at every `|` and parses each piece as JSON. A string literal containing `|`, `"` or `\` gets cut mid-literal, so the author gets an `object` control. Before #384 that prop got a radio with the right options.

**The fix.** Use the raw-name form, which gives a real boolean option, only when every member's text survives that split-and-parse. Otherwise fall back to the structured `enum` shape with the literal contents intact. In that rare case `true` is the string "true", as it was before #384, which beats losing the options. Canonical JSON doesn't change.

**The worker must show:**
- **Pre-fix proof:** tests for `'a|b' | true`, `'a"b' | true` and `'a\\b' | 1 | false` that fail first, using the control Storybook's real converter picks.
- **Guards:** `'a' | 1 | true` still gives radio `["a", 1, true]`, and `'a|b' | 'c'` is still an enum.
- **Docs:** the RDT enum section is updated if its sentence about boolean unions becomes incomplete.

**Resolving the finding.** I can't mark it resolved myself. The review re-runs on the new commit, and a clean pass clears it. If it lingers after that, I'll give you the exact dismissal command, like the earlier ones.

Still running: this fix, Batch 1 of the resolver defects, and the construct-matrix research. Waiting on you: #379, #380 (CI), #384 after this fix, and #291.

Our goal is 100% conformance, with much lower memory use and faster type checking. [Read the announcement](https://blog.cloudflare.com/typescript-rust-port/). ## Get started ```sh pnpm add -D tsrs pnpm exec tsrs --noEmit --fast ``` `--fast` enables performance optimizations, including adaptive checker counts and additional caches. See [fast mode](#fast-mode) for details. You can try `tsrs` today and give us feedback on performance, memory usage, and conformance. Try checking and emitting code in the [browser playground](https://tsrs-playground.void.app). ## Conformance We aim to release a stable version against TypeScript 7.1 with 100% conformance. See [compatibility and evidence](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/docs/COMPATIBILITY.md) for supported features and known gaps. Default mode preserves the pinned TypeScript compiler's checker behavior, including known diagnostic differences when checker count or file order changes. This sensitivity is inherited from TypeScript itself. See [differences from pinned TypeScript](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/docs/DEFAULTS.md) for the remaining runtime differences and unsupported features. ## Fast mode The following defaults and opt-in preset are available in **0.20.0** and later. By default, tsrs follows the pinned TypeScript compiler's checker settings: four checkers (capped by file count), Go's file assignment and checker history. Enable the fast preset with `--fast` or `TSRS_FAST=1`: ```sh pnpm exec tsrs --noEmit --fast # Or enable the same preset through the environment: TSRS_FAST=1 pnpm exec tsrs --noEmit ``` Fast mode adapts checker counts to the machine and project, groups related work together, and enables additional caches and memory optimizations. It keeps `strict`, `skipLibCheck`, `noCheck` and other checking options as configured. See [performance options](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/docs/USAGE.md#performance-options) for configuration, behavior and incremental-cache details. ## Extra features [`@tsrs/wasm`](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/npm/tsrs-wasm/README.md) provides WebAssembly support targeting `wasm32-wasip1` (WASI Preview 1). ## Learn more - [CLI usage and memory tuning](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/docs/USAGE.md) - [Editor setup](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/docs/LSP.md#editor-setup) - [Node API](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/docs/NODE_API.md) - [WebAssembly for Node and browsers](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/npm/tsrs-wasm/README.md) - [Benchmarks and methodology](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/bench/README.md) - [Release notes](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/docs/STATUS.md) - [Engineering notes](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/notes/README.md) ## Contributing The [issue tracker](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/issues) is open for bug reports. Please include a minimal reproduction. Pull requests remain closed because we don't have the bandwidth to review them. See the [contributing guide](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for building from source and running the suites, the [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md), and [security policy](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/blob/main/SECURITY.md) for reporting vulnerabilities. ## Acknowledgments We thank the following organizations and contributors:

content.text:
You were right, and I was wrong to say oxc had no checker. After checking upstream, oxc does have one.

**What exists.** [oxc-project/tsrs](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs) is a Rust port of the TypeScript 7 type checker. It is Apache-2.0, was created 2026-10-01, and has about 3,000 stars. It was pushed to today. The README calls it a drop-in replacement for the TypeScript 7 compiler and language server, aiming at 100% conformance with 7.1, with lower memory and faster checking ([announcement coverage](https://rustify.rs/articles/tsrs-typescript-compiler-rust-cloudflare-2026)). Pull requests are closed.

I had only looked in `oxc_*` crates and in two local copies of this project. Oxc's type-aware linting still goes through [tsgolint](https://oxc.rs/docs/guide/usage/linter/type-aware.html), which uses the Go checker. tsrs is a separate repo, which is why my crate listing missed it.

**Crates that matter for us:** `tsrs_checker`, `tsrs_binder`, `tsrs_parser`, `tsrs_api` (plus `_codec` and `_transport`), `tsrs_ipc`, `tsrs_pseudochecker` and `tsrs_declarations`.

**Why it could matter:**
- **Backend swap:** if tsrs speaks the same API as `tsgo --api`, it could replace the backend of caliper's opt-in semantic path (`crates/tsc-client`).
- **Library:** if it can be linked, caliper could ask a checker for the cases that need real instantiation.
- **`tsrs_pseudochecker`:** this is the checker-free type inference the Go port uses for declaration emit, which looks like the right tool for the "syntactic" defects.

**What I don't know yet:**
- Whether it is usable as a Rust library, or only as a binary or via npm and wasm.
- Whether its API matches what `crates/tsc-client` calls.
- Its conformance gaps for React types, its memory and speed on large projects, and the risk of a pre-1.0 project that changes daily and only takes issues.

I've sent this to the construct-matrix worker as a required part of its research, with citations, and with the smallest experiment that would prove or kill it. That experiment compares `tsrs` and `tsgo` output on one-file fixtures with no oracle run and no corpora. It was already running when I sent the correction, so I haven't seen results.

Other workers are still running: Batch 1 of the resolver defects and the `|`-in-literal projection fix.

(F2) resolver/primitives.rs:175 + resolver/evaluate.rs:791-798 `member_shared`: module `Table` declares `row: Row['value']`; factory-local props read `Table['row']` while shadowing `Row`; the member's type is returned without its declaring scope and resolved against the caller's scope (module `string` becomes local `number`). Change #176 is PR #379 (the local-interface scoping). Change #176 shows 4 open findings, not 3. All are medium, and a worker is verifying and fixing them now. I haven't seen its results yet.

**The four findings.** All are in the same place, resolving a local interface that shadows a module-level one:
1. A generic alias expanded directly (`Shared<boolean>`) bypasses `enter_alias_site`. A factory-local `Row` then replaces module `Row` inside the generic alias body.
2. An indexed member read (`Table['row']`) returns the member's type without its declaring scope. A module `string` becomes a local `number`.
3. For a generic factory returning `... as Result`, the factory's scope is attached to props that `component_props_type` already expanded. A same-named local interface replaces module `Props`.
4. Cycle detection keys on file, name and arguments only. With module `Props`, `type Outer = Props` and a local `Props extends Outer`, the distinct declarations look circular and `a` is lost.

**The pattern.** This is the second review round on this scope-passing code, so the worker fixes it once at the root. The scope in effect while resolving a declaration's body must be that declaration's own scope, not the reference site's. That is set in one place that every entry point goes through, and cycle detection keys on the resolved declaration, not just its name. The worker lists every entry point it checked.

**What the worker must do:**
- **Verify each finding first** with a failing test on real source, shown to fail on the current branch, so I can tell valid from invalid. If one doesn't reproduce, it changes no code for it and reports why.
- **Prove nothing else moved:** existing tests and snapshots unchanged, and Chakra output byte-identical to main apart from durations, with memory and time within a few percent. It won't fetch corpora, so it uses fixtures if none are installed.
- **Keep the diff small and local:** the stacked Batch 1 branch builds on this one.

**Resolving or dismissing.** If the worker confirms a finding and fixes it, the next review pass clears it. If one is invalid, I'll give you the exact dismissal command with the worker's reason, because dismissals are denied for me.

**Conflict warning.** The Batch 1 worker and this one touch overlapping resolver files. Batch 1 will need a rebase onto #379 after this lands.

Still running: this worker, Batch 1, the `|`-in-literal projection fix, and the construct-matrix research including tsrs. Waiting on you: #380 (CI), #384 after its fix, #291.

1. **List every entry point first.** Every place a declaration body is entered: interface bodies, alias bodies including generic expansion, extends chains, member and indexed access, factory results, `component_props_type`, wrapper and callee results, re-exports, and type-argument binding. The construct matrix is done, but its tsrs part is not, so I sent the worker back to do it. Its idle report still said "oxc has no type checker" because it never saw my correction. The matrix itself is at `/tmp/claude-501/ast/matrix.txt`.

**The matrix** (one row per construct, each at its worst outcome, read at main `644df655`):
- Faithful 14.
- Approximated 13.
- Opaque with `degradedBy` 10.
- Opaque with only a diagnostic or nothing 8.
- Silent or wrong families 6.
- Dropped 3.

**Silent rows, ranked by likely real-world frequency in React props** (the worker's estimate from construct shape, not measured):
1. A `Partial`, `Required`, `Omit` or `Pick` alias used as a prop type is forwarded to its base (`resolver/alias.rs:878-884`). PR #385 fixes this one.
2. `'a' | (string & {})` loses the `& {}` (`resolver/primitives.rs:105-128`).
3. A call-signature-only literal becomes `{}`, construct signatures are dropped, and a call signature beside other props vanishes (`extractor/mod.rs`). #385 covers the main cases.
4. A template-literal index key has no `degradedBy`. #385 covers it.
5. Tuple optional elements and labels are dropped (`[a: string, b?: number]` becomes `[string, number]`), and `PropType::Tuple` can't hold them.
6. A tuple rest element becomes a double array (`[string, ...number[]]` becomes `[string, number[][]]`).
7. A getter member (`get g(): T`) becomes a function field, and overloaded methods become two fields.
8. `-1`, `10n` and plain template literals are opaque but marked, so they aren't silent.
9. A mapped type's `as` clause and `readonly` modifier aren't read.

Items 5, 6 and 7 are new, and I'd put them in Batch 2. Two things from my earlier list are fine on main: `Alias<Args>['k']` and an unbound type parameter. Inline discriminated unions come out as object unions.

**Correction to my brief.** I told the worker that TypeScript does not reduce `'a' | 'b' | string`. It does reduce it to `string` (`removeRedundantLiteralTypes`, `checker.go:25732`, and a tsc 6.0.3 run prints it). `string & {}` works by turning off supertype reduction. That matters for Storybook controls, and the worker will state precisely what the checker prints for each form.

**Classification.** Syntactic means the AST text alone decides it. Structural means name lookup and substitution over the declaration graph. Needs the checker means assignability, inference or the value namespace, such as `ReturnType`, `Parameters`, `typeof f()` and conditionals over generics. Most of the silent rows are syntactic, so they can be fixed in the extractor without any checker.

**oxc itself.** The worker found `oxc_semantic` (scopes, symbols, a type/value split, enum evaluation) and `oxc_isolated_declarations` (copies annotations, infers only obvious literals, refuses the rest). The linter's type-aware mode spawns `tsgolint`, which is the same architecture as `crates/tsc-client`. A correction on `oxc-stack` and `oxc-release-builds`: they are caliper worktrees, as I said.

**Next.** The worker is doing the tsrs analysis (library or binary, protocol compatibility with `tsc-client`, `tsrs_pseudochecker`, conformance gaps for React types, memory and speed, risks, and a cheap experiment), then writing the full report to `/tmp/claude-501/ast/FINAL.txt`.

Still running: the #379 findings worker and the `|`-in-literal projection fix. Waiting on you: #379, #380, #384, #385 (after #379) and #291.

tsrs gives caliper a second checker binary for the existing opt-in semantic backend. It is not a library, and it fixes none of the extractor and resolver defects. The worker says the full report is truncated; I have the findings below, and the complete text is at `/tmp/claude-501/ast/FINAL.txt` if it wrote it.

**What the tsrs analysis found:**
- **Not linkable as a library.** Every crate is `publish = false`, so none is on crates.io. It ships only as npm packages (`tsrs`, `@tsrs/<platform>`, `@tsrs/wasm`). Linking would mean a git dependency on about 45 crates, edition 2024, Rust 1.99 (caliper pins 1.97), with no stable API.
- **Same TypeScript pin.** It ports the commit that is the `gitHead` of `typescript@7.1.0-beta`, the version caliper's backend already uses.
- **Protocol coverage.** All 19 methods that `crates/semantic/src/rpc.rs` calls are in its list. The core ones are "supported", and the checker ones are "partial" in its own matrix.
- **Matched on one-prop fixtures.** The worker swapped one import in the oracle's checker half (`typescript-beta/sync` to `tsrs/sync`) and ran 87 one-prop fixtures through both. All 87 verdicts matched, and `typeToString` was identical on every wrong or less-precise row. The worker did not run corpora.
- **Faster, lighter.** From its own benchmark on an M3 Max: Storybook's whole-project check takes 0.29 s and 446 MiB against tsgo's 0.72 s and 925 MiB. Mui-docs takes 1.45 s and 1.28 GiB against 4.06 s and 3.26 GiB. That is typically 2 to 3 times faster and about 2.1 to 2.6 times less memory, with identical diagnostics on its 19 projects. Chakra and Mantine aren't in the benchmark.
- **Conformance.** Its compatibility doc lists no mapped, conditional, indexed-access, template or intersection gaps. The listed gaps are CLI commands, profiling, a few history-dependent diagnostics and Windows ARM64.
- **`tsrs_pseudochecker`** is a port of typescript-go's declaration-emit helper. It never interprets annotations, so it does not help with the tuple, accessor, call-signature, `& {}` or alias defects.
- **Licence.** Apache-2.0 into caliper's FSL-1.1-MIT is fine for binary or npm use.

**What is not verified:**
- The async JSON-RPC framing between caliper's own client and tsrs. The worker's test was blocked, so it used the sync SDK.
- Time to first answer against the 150 ms on-demand wait.
- Behaviour on Chakra or Mantine.
- caliper's supervisor checks the binary's version against an allow-list (`crates/tsc-client/src/supervisor.rs`). `0.23.0-ts7.1.0-beta` would need adding.

**What it means for us.**
- **Experimental backend:** it could become a faster and lighter option behind the same opt-in flag. That helps the on-demand path, which waits 150 ms before taking the structural answer.
- **Defects:** the silent-wrong families in the matrix are caliper's own extractor and resolver bugs. They stay regardless.
- **Precondition:** the TS 7.1 backend stays experimental and off by default. Making any checker the default would need oracle evidence and a new ADR.

**Cheapest next experiment, no oracle and no corpora.** Run caliper's `--experimental-semantic-types` path with `tsc_path` pointed at the tsrs binary, on the same fixtures, compare caliper's JSON, and time the first answer on one Chakra-sized project. Do you want me to run it? It is a small worker with a handful of commands.

Still running: the #379 findings worker and the `|`-in-literal projection fix. Waiting on you: #379, #380, #384, #385 (after #379) and #291.

# Rust practices

`docs/PORTING.md` says how Go becomes Rust. This file says what the Rust must not do, how that is checked, and which
performance techniques are in place, rejected or untried.

The Clippy baseline follows oxc's `all`, `pedantic`, `complexity`, `nursery`, and `cargo` groups, with the
remaining global exceptions documented in `Cargo.toml`. The port keeps the Go source's API structure, vocabulary, numeric
domains, and control-flow shape where changing them would obscure parity, so `Cargo.toml` documents the additional
active exceptions. The stricter rules below target costs and risks that a port can introduce: copies, allocations,
argument passing, hash iteration order, threading, and `unsafe`. They draw on Bun, oxc, Rolldown, rust-analyzer, Ruff
and ty, Biome, Turborepo, and swc. Where a rule copies one of them, it says which.

Rust naming lints are denied: types and traits use UpperCamelCase, functions and fields use snake_case, and constants
and statics use SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE. Bitflags types and constants keep their upstream names. Upstream acronym spellings
remain (`ID`, `APIState`, `JSX`), with local reasoned Clippy expectations where needed. Serialized names, diagnostics
and native ABI symbols keep their upstream spelling.

## Clippy

```sh
cargo clippy --all-targets --config 'build.warnings="deny"'
```

`[workspace.lints.clippy]` in `Cargo.toml` and `clippy.toml` turn on the oxc baseline and the project-specific strict
lints, all at `deny`. The command also rejects ordinary compiler warnings. There is no findings baseline:
the command above must be clean before a change lands (CI runs it in the `lint` job).

When it fails:

- Fix the finding. `cargo +<toolchain> clippy -p <crate>` shows clippy's suggestion.
- If the flagged code is intended, put `#[expect(clippy::<lint>, reason = "...")]` on the smallest item or statement
  that covers it. The reason is for the next reader; for `inline_always` and the unchecked operations it cites the
  measurement. Use `#[expect]`, not `#[allow]`: it warns once the lint stops firing, so a suppression cannot outlive
  its cause. A bare `#[allow]` is itself a finding.

Details:

- Findings depend on the Clippy version, so `rust-toolchain.toml` pins it everywhere.
- Run from the repository root, where Cargo selects every workspace crate by default. The command covers all
  targets, including tests and examples. The Fourslash task package is included; the upstream Go suite runs
  through `tools/go-fourslash` without generating Rust fixtures.
- Also check `--all-features` when changing lint policy. It enables `plain-ptrs`, so check optional features with
  compressed pointers separately. These scopes include profiling tools and both pointer representations.
- Workspace crates declare `publish = false`; missing crates.io metadata does not need a global exception.
- Generated Rust is linted; fix its generator when Clippy finds something. When generated code intentionally needs
  an exception, emit the smallest reasoned `#[expect]` from the generator.
- `dead_code`, `unused_imports`, `unused_variables`, `unused_mut` and `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` are ordinary compiler
  warnings, which `build.warnings=deny` rejects.

## Upgrading Rust

`Cargo.toml` declares the same MSRV that `rust-toolchain.toml` pins for local builds, CI, clippy, the bench and
releases; every workspace crate inherits it and every workflow installs it. Floating stable would change the
compiler under the bench every six weeks, and the regression flag would blame whichever pull request merged next.
An upgrade is a pull request of its own:

1. Change `rust-version` in `Cargo.toml` and `channel` in `rust-toolchain.toml` together.
2. Fix what the new compiler rejects (CI sets Cargo's `build.warnings=deny`).
3. Run the full Clippy command above on macOS and Linux and fix every new finding.
4. Measure the instruction and peak-memory change per project before and after the upgrade and put it in the pull

The Clippy baseline follows oxc's `all`, `pedantic`, `complexity`, `nursery`, and `cargo` groups, with the
remaining global exceptions documented in `Cargo.toml`. The port keeps the Go source's API structure, vocabulary, numeric
domains, and control-flow shape where changing them would obscure parity, so `Cargo.toml` documents the additional
active exceptions. The stricter rules below target costs and risks that a port can introduce: copies, allocations,
argument passing, hash iteration order, threading, and `unsafe`. They draw on Bun, oxc, Rolldown, rust-analyzer, Ruff
and ty, Biome, Turborepo, and swc. Where a rule copies one of them, it says which.

Rust naming lints are denied: types and traits use UpperCamelCase, functions and fields use snake_case, and constants
and statics use SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE. Bitflags types and constants keep their upstream names. Upstream acronym spellings
remain (`ID`, `APIState`, `JSX`), with local reasoned Clippy expectations where needed. Serialized names, diagnostics
and native ABI symbols keep their upstream spelling.

## Clippy

```sh
cargo clippy --all-targets --config 'build.warnings="deny"'
```

`[workspace.lints.clippy]` in `Cargo.toml` and `clippy.toml` turn on the oxc baseline and the project-specific strict
lints, all at `deny`. The command also rejects ordinary compiler warnings. There is no findings baseline:
the command above must be clean before a change lands (CI runs it in the `lint` job).

When it fails:

- Fix the finding. `cargo +<toolchain> clippy -p <crate>` shows clippy's suggestion.
- If the flagged code is intended, put `#[expect(clippy::<lint>, reason = "...")]` on the smallest item or statement
  that covers it. The reason is for the next reader; for `inline_always` and the unchecked operations it cites the
  measurement. Use `#[expect]`, not `#[allow]`: it warns once the lint stops firing, so a suppression cannot outlive
  its cause. A bare `#[allow]` is itself a finding.

Details:

- Findings depend on the Clippy version, so `rust-toolchain.toml` pins it everywhere.
- Run from the repository root, where Cargo selects every workspace crate by default. The command covers all
  targets, including tests and examples. The Fourslash task package is included; the upstream Go suite runs
  through `tools/go-fourslash` without generating Rust fixtures.
- Also check `--all-features` when changing lint policy. It enables `plain-ptrs`, so check optional features with
  compressed pointers separately. These scopes include profiling tools and both pointer representations.
- Workspace crates declare `publish = false`; missing crates.io metadata does not need a global exception.
- Generated Rust is linted; fix its generator when Clippy finds something. When generated code intentionally needs
  an exception, emit the smallest reasoned `#[expect]` from the generator.
- `dead_code`, `unused_imports`, `unused_variables`, `unused_mut` and `unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn` are ordinary compiler
  warnings, which `build.warnings=deny` rejects.

## Integration contract (Rust)

### Session boundary (core, `tsrs_api::handler`)

```rust
pub enum Response { Json(String), Binary(Vec<u8>) }   // Go `any` result / `RawBinary`
pub struct ApiError { pub kind: ErrorKind, pub message: String } // Display == Go err.Error()
pub enum ErrorKind { InvalidRequest, ClientError, Unsupported, Internal }
pub trait Handler: Send + Sync {                         // Go ipc.Handler
    fn handle_request(&self, method: &str, params: &[u8]) -> ApiResult<Response>; // params = raw JSON bytes ("" = absent)
    fn handle_notification(&self, method: &str, params: &[u8]) -> ApiResult<()>;
}
pub trait ClientConn: Send + Sync {                      // Go ipc.Conn.Call (server -> client)
    fn call(&self, method: &str, params: &str) -> ApiResult<String>; // JSON text in/out
}
tsrs_api::Session::new(SessionOptions { cwd, default_library_path, fs, binary_responses, run_external_code }) -> Arc<Session>
session.set_connection(Arc<dyn ClientConn>); session.close();  // Session: Handler
```

- `binary_responses` is true for the sync MessagePack protocol (Go `UseBinaryResponses`); source-file
  responses are then `Response::Binary`, otherwise `{"data": base64}` JSON.
- `echo` and `ping` are handled before method lookup exactly like Go. Unknown methods are
  `InvalidRequest` (`unknown API method "x"`).
- Both protocols put errors on the wire as `jsonrpc.CodeInternalError` with `err.to_string()`.
- Handler panics are caught and returned as `panic: ...` errors (Go conn recovers too).

### Runtime (`tsrs_api_transport`)

The transport does not depend on `tsrs_api`. It defines its own handler/conn traits with the same shape;
`crates/tsrs_cli/src/api.rs` (core) adapts them. Entry points:

- a sync conn running the msgpack `[type, method, payload]` tuple protocol over stdin/stdout or a pipe,
  supporting re-entrant `call` from inside a request (filesystem callbacks), with concurrent
  callbacks answering nested requests in stack order, and an async JSON-RPC conn
  with concurrent request dispatch and outstanding server->client calls;
- `RawBinary`-equivalent results written as msgpack `bin`; `getServerTiming`/`resetServerTiming`
  handled in the conn as in Go `ipc/timing.go`;
- deterministic shutdown: EOF on input ends `run` with `Ok`, malformed frames end it with an error
  without writing non-protocol bytes to stdout.

`--api --pipe <path>` creates a new private directory on Unix, with a socket at
`<path>/socket` (`0700` directory, `0600` socket); an existing path is an error. On Windows,
`<path>` is a named pipe restricted to the current user. The spawned sync client gives its
Windows pipe a random 128-bit suffix. LSP `custom/initializeAPISession` returns the same private pipe transport for an API session over the language
server's project session; an API-client disconnect releases its resources, and an explicit LSP shutdown stops pending
and connected sessions. Like pinned Go (`3e9236361fa9`), LSP EOF or context cancellation alone does not stop a
pending API accept. Its listener remains until explicitly stopped or the process exits, and the private Unix socket
directory survives process exit. See the [LSP known gaps](LSP.md#known-gaps).
`getCurrentLanguageServerSnapshot` flushes pending editor changes and applies the API client's opens, closes and
program changes. Each client owns its open references and synthetic programs; closing it releases those resources.

content.text:
Yes, it would simplify a lot, and the crates may not be coming at all. Here is what I found.

**Are the crates coming?** There is no sign of it.
- **Workspace setting:** the workspace sets `publish = false`, and the repo's `docs/RUST.md` says every crate declares it.
- **The one request:** [issue #858 "publish crates through crates.io"](https://github.com/oxc-project/tsrs/issues/858) has been open since 2026-10-30 from someone who wants the checker as a library. It has two comments, an automation bot's triage and no maintainer reply. The bot calls it a release-infrastructure decision for the maintainers.
- **Pull requests are closed.** We can't contribute the change ourselves.

**Linking to version tags works without crates.io.** The repo has tags `v0.15.0` to `v0.23.0`, with a release every two or three days. A Cargo git dependency pinned by `tag = "v0.23.0"` is possible, since `publish = false` only blocks crates.io. I haven't built it.

**An in-process Rust API is documented.** `docs/NODE_API.md` has an "Integration contract (Rust)" section: `tsrs_api::Session::new(SessionOptions { cwd, default_library_path, fs, ... }) -> Arc<Session>`, where `Session` implements `Handler::handle_request(method, params)`. These are the same method names caliper already sends over the process boundary, minus the transport.

**What we'd gain** by dropping the process:
- No spawn, no framing and no supervisor.
- No separate address space for the checker, so lower memory and no startup wait.
- Most of the machinery we've been fixing goes away: disconnect diagnostics, `InvalidJson`, the timeout paths, the version allow-list.

**What it costs:**
- **Isolation.** The process boundary contains a checker abort or stack overflow, which would otherwise kill the Storybook dev server. tsrs says handler panics are caught, but aborts are not panics.
- **Toolchain and build.** The workspace needs Rust 1.99 and edition 2024 (caliper pins 1.97). It is about 45 crates, which adds compile time and binary size to the napi addon, plus its own allocator setup.
- **Memory model.** Source files are `&'static`, with an arena and a poison mode. Whether a long-running dev process frees memory when a session closes needs checking.
- **No stability promise.** The API is internal, releases come every few days, and bumping a tag is port work each time.
- **Parsing twice.** tsrs has its own parser, so caliper's oxc parse still runs alongside it.

**Recommendation.** Run a bounded spike before any commitment, with no oracle and no corpora. In a scratch branch, add the git dependency at `v0.23.0`, build `tsrs_api` alone, create a `Session`, call the 19 methods on fixtures, and report compile time, binary size, resident memory after close, and time to first answer against the 150 ms wait. The process mode stays as the fallback until those numbers are in. If the spike is clean, we'd write the ADR.

I can also ask the maintainers on issue #858 whether publishing is planned. That is a public comment under your account, so I won't post it without your say.

Do you want the spike?

The post doesn't address crates.io publishing, using the checker as a Rust library, or a 1.0 release. It does address roadmap and maintenance, though only in general terms.

- **Crates.io, library use, or embedding:** Not mentioned. The only distribution method named is npm: "You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm." The post also describes running development environments via WebAssembly, saying you can "run those environments safely client-side in your browser."
- **API stability:** Not mentioned. The closest statement is that "A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible."
- **Roadmap:** Partial. Known differences from upstream will be reduced before a stable release: "We aim to reduce those differences to a minimum by the time we publish a stable release." The post also says the team will "attempt to contribute them back to the TypeScript Go codebase" when it finds performance improvements.
- **Stable 1.0 release:** Not mentioned. The only reference is the "stable release" quoted above, with no version number.
- **Maintenance:** Partial. The post says "Like with Vinext, our goal is to run tsrs as a well-maintained healthy open source project." It also says "The Oxc team has already begun refactoring the codebase to make it faster, use less memory, and make it maintainable." Plans include merging with tsc-rs "into a single package" with Theo Browne. The post says "the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like" regarding the language.

These notes record measurements, design decisions, regressions and approaches that did not work. They are
evidence from a particular revision and machine; the [compatibility table](../docs/COMPATIBILITY.md) describes
current capabilities, and the [release notes](../docs/STATUS.md) describe shipped changes.

## Reading historical results

Compiler defaults, source pins, commands, tool paths and open questions in a note belong to the revision it
records. For current behavior and commands, start with [usage](../docs/USAGE.md),
[contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md) and [debugging](../docs/DEBUGGING.md).

Since 0.20.0, ordinary compilation uses pinned TypeScript's checker settings; adaptive checker counts and the
additional performance modes require `--fast` or an explicit feature override. Older notes often call those
settings the default. See [performance options](../docs/USAGE.md#performance-options) when comparing runs.

Older acceptance percentages are historical decision criteria. The current
[measurement policy](../AGENTS.md#performance-and-memory-changes) has no fixed minimum percentage: repeatable
improvements across most catalog projects, or a significant repeatable improvement on one, may be accepted.
An idea rejected only for missing an old threshold can be revisited; correctness failures and measured
regressions still need to be addressed.

Allocation profiles and reachability-census results in older notes came from tooling that has been removed.
Their measurements remain historical evidence. For supported memory reports and ownership checks, use the
[current debugging guide](../docs/DEBUGGING.md#arena-recycling-checks).

Completed experiments' build wrappers, AST sizing table scripts and Node API probes and audit logs have also been
removed. Their last versions are available at commit `b620e8e5` (for example,
`git show b620e8e5:tools/sizing/compact_ast.py`). References to them below are historical; reusable measurement

- **Crates.io, library use, or embedding:** Not mentioned. The only distribution method named is npm: "You can try an experimental release by installing the tsrs package from npm." The post also describes running development environments via WebAssembly, saying you can "run those environments safely client-side in your browser."
- **API stability:** Not mentioned. The closest statement is that "A Rust port has to follow those decisions closely, or it will eventually fall apart and become incompatible."
- **Roadmap:** Partial. Known differences from upstream will be reduced before a stable release: "We aim to reduce those differences to a minimum by the time we publish a stable release." The post also says the team will "attempt to contribute them back to the TypeScript Go codebase" when it finds performance improvements.
- **Stable 1.0 release:** Not mentioned. The only reference is the "stable release" quoted above, with no version number.
- **Maintenance:** Partial. The post says "Like with Vinext, our goal is to run tsrs as a well-maintained healthy open source project." It also says "The Oxc team has already begun refactoring the codebase to make it faster, use less memory, and make it maintainable." Plans include merging with tsc-rs "into a single package" with Theo Browne. The post says "the TypeScript team should remain solely responsible for deciding what that looks like" regarding the language.

# Engineering notes

These notes record measurements, design decisions, regressions and approaches that did not work. They are
evidence from a particular revision and machine; the [compatibility table](../docs/COMPATIBILITY.md) describes
current capabilities, and the [release notes](../docs/STATUS.md) describe shipped changes.

## Reading historical results

Compiler defaults, source pins, commands, tool paths and open questions in a note belong to the revision it
records. For current behavior and commands, start with [usage](../docs/USAGE.md),
[contributing](../CONTRIBUTING.md) and [debugging](../docs/DEBUGGING.md).

Since 0.20.0, ordinary compilation uses pinned TypeScript's checker settings; adaptive checker counts and the
additional performance modes require `--fast` or an explicit feature override. Older notes often call those
settings the default. See [performance options](../docs/USAGE.md#performance-options) when comparing runs.

Older acceptance percentages are historical decision criteria. The current
[measurement policy](../AGENTS.md#performance-and-memory-changes) has no fixed minimum percentage: repeatable
improvements across most catalog projects, or a significant repeatable improvement on one, may be accepted.
An idea rejected only for missing an old threshold can be revisited; correctness failures and measured
regressions still need to be addressed.

Allocation profiles and reachability-census results in older notes came from tooling that has been removed.
Their measurements remain historical evidence. For supported memory reports and ownership checks, use the
[current debugging guide](../docs/DEBUGGING.md#arena-recycling-checks).

Completed experiments' build wrappers, AST sizing table scripts and Node API probes and audit logs have also been
removed. Their last versions are available at commit `b620e8e5` (for example,
`git show b620e8e5:tools/sizing/compact_ast.py`). References to them below are historical; reusable measurement
tools, code generators and regression harnesses remain in `tools/`.

content.text:
**On tsrs: I found no evidence that crates are coming.** I checked the Cloudflare announcement, the issues and the docs.

- **The announcement** names npm as the only distribution channel, and the post never mentions crates.io, library use or API stability. It says the goal is a "well-maintained healthy open source project", and that the Oxc team is already refactoring for speed, memory and maintainability. It plans to merge with tsc-rs "into a single package" and to contribute performance fixes back to TypeScript Go. It also says known differences from upstream will be reduced before a stable release.
- **Issue #858 (publish to crates.io)** has been open since 2026-10-30 with only a triage bot's comment and no maintainer reply. The bot says maintainers would need to discuss "crates.io publication, versioning, and API stability" first.
- **Issue #871 ("Long-term vision")** asks whether tsrs will become the official compiler. It is also open with only a bot reply and no maintainer answer.
- **The docs** have no roadmap and no plan to publish. `docs/STATUS.md` release notes talk about npm packages only. There are no GitHub discussions.

**What helps:**
- **Release cadence:** version tags `v0.15.0` to `v0.23.0` land every two or three days, so a git dependency pinned to a tag is realistic.
- **In-process Rust API:** the documented `tsrs_api::Session` would let us drop the process boundary.
- **Stable-release target:** the post says a stable release is the point where differences from TypeScript get minimized. That is the natural moment to look again at library use.

**My read.** Don't bet on crates.io. A tag-pinned git dependency is the only realistic route, and it carries the isolation, toolchain and build costs I listed. If you want a signal, I can post a short, specific question on #858. It is a public comment under your account, so I won't without your say.

**PR #384:** the `|` fix is pushed (`0bfc258b`, signed). A union with a boolean member stays a raw name only if every member's text survives Storybook's split and parse. Otherwise it stays an `enum` with each member's raw text. In the worker's runs, `'a|b' | true` and `'a"b' | true` now give enum options instead of an `object` control. A backslash case that corrupted the literal now keeps it. Guards pass, the clean-room run is 1294 passed, and lint and `just semver` exit 0. CI is green except Coverage and Entire Gates, which are pending. I updated the PR body to describe the exception.

The #379 findings worker is still running. Waiting on you: #379, #380, #384, #385 (after #379) and #291, plus whether you want the tsrs spike.

content.content:
## Next step

Slice 1 below covers function components by their export. Next, in order: set what `PropType` now carries (optional and rest parameters, index signatures, `readonly`, a ref type's name), per-prop `tags` and `parent`, class and generic components, `batchRequests` to cut round trips and watch-mode notifications. The NAPI binding already ships: a session asks a warm checker for the requested component (`semanticTypes: 'on-demand'`, ADR 0022). The client's open Lifecycle items in the Gates table still stand.

Some props can't be resolved from the AST alone. An opt-in backend asks TypeScript's checker instead, using the algorithm react-docgen-typescript (RDT) uses, and merges the answer into the structural result. Structural extraction stays the default.

## What the structural resolver can't do

Component prop counts from `fixtures/` with `--html-attributes full`, against RDT. Root causes are from `docs/benchmarks.md`.

| Gap | Example | Ours | RDT |
| --- | --- | --: | --: |
| Generics through alias chains | ariakit `Props<T, O> = O & Omit<ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T>, keyof O>` | 5 | 294 |
| Generics through alias chains | ark-ui `SelectRoot` | 36 | 314 |

2. **`ref` and `key`.** RDT emits both, and nothing else records forwardRef metadata. Semantic mode must match whatever the structural path does.

Short answer: keep our parser and extractor for now, make tsrs the checker behind the path that already exists, and decide on a checker-first default with measurements. Here is the architecture as I see it. I verified the sizes below by cloning tsrs at `v0.23.0`.

**What we maintain today.** The extractor is 5.4k lines and the structural resolver is 7.9k, with 4.5k of types and 3.4k of pipeline and 18.9k lines of tests behind them. The resolver approximates a type checker, and it is where every defect we've chased came from: scoping, alias wrappers, call signatures, intersections. The checker path (`crates/semantic` and `crates/tsc-client`, 2.4k lines) is opt-in. The current design table puts a Go-checker spawn at 33 to 72 ms and about 100 MB, against 50 ms for the whole structural run.

**Do we need all the crates?** For types, yes.
- **Checker:** `tsrs_checker` is about 109k lines, and the documented `Session` API pulls 31 of the 43 workspace crates.
- **Parse only:** `tsrs_parser` needs just 6 crates, about 64k lines, mostly the AST.
- **Toolchain:** the workspace wants Rust 1.99 and edition 2024. This machine has 1.98.1, so we'd upgrade, which I agree we should anyway.

**Their parser or ours?** Keep oxc.
- Our extractor and its 18.9k lines of tests are written against `oxc_ast`.
- tsrs's AST is a port of the Go one, with no stability promise.
- A shared parse isn't available: `Session` builds its own programs from disk, so we'd parse twice either way.
- If we want real scoping for ADR 0025, `oxc_semantic` gives scopes and symbols on the AST we already have.

**Recommended direction, staged with gates:**
1. **Now, small.** Allow the tsrs binary in the existing supervisor (one version-allow-list line). The worker's 87 fixtures matched the Go checker, and tsrs reports 2 to 3 times faster and about half the memory. Verify the async framing with caliper's real client.
2. **Spike, no oracle.** Measure an in-process `Session` through a tag-pinned git dependency: compile time, binary size, resident memory after close, and time to first answer on a Chakra-sized project. Compare with the process mode.
3. **Decision (new ADR).** If the numbers hold, make the checker the default arbiter for the CLI and agent surface, where a spawn is affordable. In Storybook the structural result stays the instant first answer and the checker answer arrives later, which is what ADR 0022 already does. That follows your priority: correct types first, first load imperceptible.

**What this changes in the current work.** Keep the silent-wrong fixes and the review-finding fixes. Hold the deeper structural scoping branches (ADR 0025 branches 3 to 5) and threading scope through the evaluator's 26 call sites until the gate-3 decision. Those are the pieces a checker-first default would make least valuable.

**Not verified.** The in-process build and size costs, the async framing, time-to-first-answer against the 150 ms wait, and behaviour on large projects. That is what the spike is for.

Should I start the spike as one worker, with no oracle and no corpora?

import subprocess,json
b=json.loads(subprocess.run(['gh','pr','view','379','--json','body'],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout)['body']
add="""
Review round (four findings, all reproduced): a declaration's body was read in the reference site's scope instead of its own. One table test, `a_declaration_body_is_read_in_its_own_scope_by_every_entry_point`, has 10 real-source rows; 7 fail on the earlier tip. The invariant is that the scope in effect while a declaration body resolves is the scope it was declared in, and a type argument keeps the scope it was written in. It is enforced through `ResolveState::enter_declared_in`, now called on three paths that lacked it (direct generic alias expansion, member reads, and factory results through `component_props_type`). Cycle identity in `resolve_props_chain` now includes the reference scope. A fifth case from the same pattern, a local interface passed as a type argument to a module generic, is fixed too. On Chakra (installed corpus) wall time is 0.26 s on both and peak RSS is 411.09 MB on main against 410.98 MB on the branch, with identical JSON apart from durations. Clean-room `cargo nextest` 1298 passed, 1 skipped.
"""
i=b.rfind('Trail:')
b=b[:i]+add.strip()+"\n\n"+b[i:]
open('/tmp/claude-501/trails3/pr379-body2.md','w').write(b)
EOF

Change #176 (PR #379) now has the fix for all four findings (commit `fc430ec7`, signed). Its CI isn't finished yet, so it isn't ready to merge.

**What the worker found.**
- **All four findings were real.** A table test with 10 real-source rows fails on 7 of them at the old tip and passes after the fix.
- **A fifth case of the same pattern.** A local interface passed as a type argument to a module generic bound to the module's version. That is fixed too.
- **The root cause.** A declaration's body was read in the scope of the reference site, not the scope it was declared in. The rule is now that the scope in effect while a body resolves is the one it was declared in, and a type argument keeps the scope it was written in. It is enforced through `ResolveState::enter_declared_in`, which three paths had been skipping. Those are direct generic alias expansion, member reads, and factory results. Cycle detection now includes the reference scope.

**Evidence.**
- **Chakra (installed corpus):** wall time 0.26 s on both main and the branch, peak RSS 411.09 MB against 410.98 MB, and identical JSON apart from durations.
- **Clean-room run:** 1298 passed, 1 skipped.
- **Lint and `just semver`:** both exit 0, and the cache version is unchanged.

**Not covered.** The evaluator's reads other than an indexed access (`keyof`, conditional and mapped types) still take no scope. That is the documented limit, and it is the piece the architecture decision may make obsolete.

**Findings status.** The review still lists 2 open findings, F1 and F4. Both point at the old code version (`01M6VVHXS1SYJ9JV84256WYNED`), so they are stale until the review re-runs on the new commit. F2 and F3 already cleared. I'll check again when Entire Gates completes, and give you the exact dismissal commands only if one lingers.

- I updated the PR body with the review round.
- #385 (stacked on this) needs a rebase onto it once #379 merges. I'll do that with a worker after your merge.
- #384's `|` fix and #380's comparator fix are in. Both are waiting on CI and your review.

python3 -I - <<'EOF'
import subprocess,os,re
files=[l.strip() for l in open(os.environ['TMPDIR']+'/files.txt') if '/resolver/' in l or '/extractor/' in l or 'types/' in l or 'toon' in l or 'pipeline/rdt' in l]
fns=[]
for f in files:
    s=subprocess.run(['git','show','origin/main:'+f],capture_output=True,text=True).stdout.splitlines()
    i=0
    while i<len(s):
        m=re.match(r'\s*(pub(\([a-z]+\))?\s+)?(async\s+)?fn\s+(\w+)',s[i])
        if m:
            # signature params until ')' at depth 0 of paren
            sig='';j=i
            while j<len(s) and '{' not in s[j] and ';' not in s[j]: sig+=s[j];j+=1
            sig+=s[j] if j<len(s) else ''
            params=sig.split('(',1)[1] if '(' in sig else ''
            depth=0;n=0;cur=''
            for ch in params:
                if ch in '(<[': depth+=1
                elif ch in ')>]':
                    if depth==0: break
                    depth-=1
                elif ch==',' and depth==0: n+=1;cur=''
                else: cur+=ch
            args=n+(1 if cur.strip() else 0)
            # body length by brace matching
            d=0;k=j;started=False
            while k<len(s):
                for ch in s[k]:
                    if ch=='{': d+=1;started=True
                    elif ch=='}': d-=1
                if started and d==0: break
                k+=1
            fns.append((k-i+1,args,m.group(4),f.replace('crates/core/src/','')+':'+str(i+1)))
            i=j+1
        else: i+=1
print('functions scanned',len(fns))
print('longest functions:')
for l,a,n,w in sorted(fns,reverse=True)[:10]: print(f'  {l:4d} lines {a} params {n} {w}')
print('most parameters:')
for l,a,n,w in sorted(fns,key=lambda x:-x[1])[:10]: print(f'  {a} params {l} lines {n} {w}')
print('functions with >=6 params:',sum(1 for x in fns if x[1]>=6),' >100 lines:',sum(1 for x in fns if x[0]>100))
EOF

            sig='';j=i
            while j<len(s) and '{' not in s[j] and ';' not in s[j]: sig+=s[j];j+=1

            params=sig.split('(',1)[1] if '(' in sig else ''
            depth=0;n=0;cur=''
            for ch in params:
                if ch in '(<[': depth+=1
                elif ch in ')>]':
                    if depth==0: break
                    depth-=1
                elif ch==',' and depth==0: n+=1;cur=''
                else: cur+=ch
            args=n+(1 if cur.strip() else 0)
            # body length by brace matching
            d=0;k=j;started=False
            while k<len(s):
                for ch in s[k]:
                    if ch=='{': d+=1;started=True
                    elif ch=='}': d-=1
                if started and d==0: break
                k+=1
            fns.append((k-i+1,args,m.group(4),f.replace('crates/core/src/','')+':'+str(i+1)))
            i=j+1

lastPrompt: Damn, our extractor is so many lines? and our structural resolver? What adjustments, reorganization and restructing could we do in the process? Any simplifications?

content.text:
Yes, it is a lot. Real code is about 6.7k lines in the resolver and 4.6k in the extractor, after excluding comments and blanks. Those lines are mostly our own approximation of a type checker, and that approximation is where nearly every defect we fixed today came from.

**Where the weight is** (code lines, origin/main):
- `types/collected.rs` 1,346, `dependency_types.rs` 1,185, `types/output.rs` 1,027, `extractor/mod.rs` 1,037, `resolver/mod.rs` 980.
- `resolver/alias.rs` 844, `extractor/component.rs` 739, `resolver/evaluate.rs` 775, `pipeline/revision.rs` 734.
- Of 705 functions scanned, 19 are over 100 lines. The longest are `resolve_props_chain` (280), `resolve_named_uncycled` (237), `resolve_base_as_chain` (221) and `classify_type_alias` (206).
- 25 functions take six or more parameters, up to nine, such as `known_fallback` and `expand_alias`.

**Simplifications, from the defects we just fixed:**
1. **One context object instead of parameter threading.** Those 25 functions pass `(file, scope, args, depth, ...)` by hand. That is exactly how scope got lost in the four #379 findings and in the evaluator's 26 scope-less call sites. A single `Ctx { file, scope, args, depth }` passed through makes "forgot the scope" impossible by construction. This is the highest-value change, and it is mostly mechanical.
2. **One declaration table.** Interfaces, aliases, enums and classes are collected and looked up by separate paths. Only the interface collector knew about `local_depth`, which is why aliases and enums still collide. A single `Declaration` table keyed by scope and name, with one lookup function, deletes the per-kind duplication. ADR 0025 branches 3 to 5 become one change.
3. **One constructor for each shape.** `Partial` and friends were built in two places and disagreed. A single `utility_wrapper(name, args)` used by both paths removes that class of bug.
4. **One projection model.** `output.rs` (1,027 lines), `toon.rs` (680) and `rdt.rs` each walk `PropType` with their own rules. The recent single-literal, boolean and truncation bugs were all divergence between them. A shared "display model" (options, literal extraction, display name) used by all three means one fix instead of three.
5. **Split by ownership, not by size.** `collected.rs` mixes the extractor's output, the merged global data, and serialization. `dependency_types.rs` mixes dependency loading, the index file and panic containment. Splitting these costs little and makes each file's job obvious. It is organization, with no behavior change.
6. **Break up the 19 long functions** along the construct matrix: one function per type construct, instead of one 280-line match.

**The larger lever** is the architecture decision from earlier. If the checker becomes the default arbiter for the CLI and agent surface, the structural resolver turns into the fast path plus fallback. Conditional types, mapped types, indexed access and generic instantiation (`evaluate.rs` and most of `alias.rs`) would not need to be perfect. My rough estimate is that a third to a half of the 6.7k resolver lines could go, but I haven't measured that. It is speculative until the spike and the ADR.

**Suggested order, one change at a time on shared files:**
1. The `Ctx` object (the mechanical, safe one), right after #379 and #385 merge.
2. The declaration table, which absorbs ADR 0025 branches 3 to 5.
3. The shared projection model.
4. File splits and the long-function breakup, interleaved.

Everything else waits on the checker-first decision. Do you want me to turn this into a trail with those steps?

input.description: Measure pattern candidates: string keys, fallthrough arms, state threading, traits

lastPrompt: Any traits or other rust pattern we should adopt here and why?

content.text:
Yes, a handful, each tied to a defect we actually hit today. The counts are from `origin/main`; the rest is my judgement.

**What the code shows now:**
- 757 mentions of `PropType::` across core.
- 167 `_ =>` fallthrough arms in the resolver and extractor.
- 78 string-keyed maps, and 17 keys built with `format!` (such as `file:Name@f0.b1`).
- 52 places that pass `&mut ResolveState`.
- Only 3 traits in core, none of them for the type model.

**Patterns to adopt, in order of value:**
1. **Newtypes for keys instead of strings.** Define `DeclKey { file, name, scope }` with `Display` for cache and debug output only. Today a key is a formatted string that gets parsed and compared by prefix. That is how a local `Row` and a module `Row` collided, and how cycle detection ignored scope (finding F4). With a typed key the compiler checks every lookup and cycle check, and `HashMap<DeclKey, _>` replaces 78 string maps over time.
2. **Exhaustive matches, no `_ =>` on the type model.** The 167 wildcard arms are where silent drops live (the matrix found call signatures, tuple elements and getters this way). Replace them with explicit arms, or a `#[deny(clippy::wildcard_enum_match_arm)]` on those modules, so a new `PropType` or AST variant forces a decision. This is the cheapest guard against the "silent wrong" family.
3. **A context struct, not threaded parameters.** `Ctx { file, scope, args, depth }`, passed as one `&Ctx`. The invariant "enter the declaration's own scope" then lives in one method (`ctx.entering(decl)`) that returns a new context. That is the single enforcement point #379's findings needed, and the compiler enforces it.
4. **A projection trait for the three outputs.** Something like `trait Projection { fn literal_option(&self, ..); fn named(&self, ..); fn opaque(&self, ..) }` with a shared `fn project<P: Projection>(ty: &PropType, p: &mut P)` walker. Canonical JSON, TOON and RDT implement the leaf rules, and the traversal lives once. The recent TOON truncation, single-literal and boolean bugs were each one projection disagreeing with another.
5. **Make illegal states unrepresentable.** The empty-object result for a call-signature-only literal, and `Raw` as a catch-all, exist because the type model has nowhere to put those cases. Add the variants (callable, opaque with a reason) so the compiler makes every consumer handle them. Tuples with optional and rest elements are the same pattern (the matrix found they are dropped today).
6. **`#[non_exhaustive]` and sealed traits on public types only.** It helps the public crates, where we just paid for the SemVer breaks. Not worth adding on internals.

**Where I'd stay away:**
- A `Resolver` trait with multiple implementations. We have one resolver, and the backend question is better handled by the existing `SemanticProvider` boundary.
- Trait objects on the hot path. The structural run's 50 ms budget favours static dispatch.
- A visitor framework or macros. The projection trait above is the proportionate version.

**Why this order.** Items 1 to 3 are mechanical and remove whole bug classes by construction, so they pay off even if we later make the checker the default. Item 4 fixes the output divergence. Item 5 goes with the construct-matrix fixes in Batch 2. I'd fold items 1 to 3 into the restructuring steps I proposed, starting right after #379 and #385 merge.

Want me to add these to trail #255 as the first restructuring batch?

lastPrompt: How does all of this pair with the tsrs codebase? What can we leverage from their side to simplify everything?

content.text:
It pairs well. The key finding is that tsrs's API already exposes the type structure our resolver approximates, so the best use is as the type authority, not as a parser or AST to adopt. I read its documented method list (`docs/NODE_API.md` at `v0.23.0`) and the crate layout.

**What its API gives us** (structured types, not strings):
- **Instantiated types:** `getPropertiesOfType`, `getSignaturesOfType`, `getParametersOfSignature`, `getIndexInfosOfType`, `getBaseTypes` and `getConstraintOfType`.
- **Alias identity:** `getAliasSymbolOfType` and `getAliasTypeArgumentsOfType`, which is where an alias name like `Partial<…>` comes from.
- **Conditional and mapped types:** `getCheckTypeOfType`, `getExtendsTypeOfType`, `getConstraintTypeOfMappedType` and `getNameTypeOfMappedType`.
- **Docs:** `getJsDocTags`, `getDocumentationComment` and `getDeclaredTypeOfSymbol`.
- **Declarations:** `getDeclarationEmit`, plus symbols and module resolution (`getSymbolAtLocation`, `getExportsOfModule`, `getResolvedModule`).

**What we could stop owning if the checker is the type authority** (my estimate of the scope, not measured):
- **Scoping, ADR 0025:** the checker's symbols answer "which declaration does this name mean", so the declaration table and scope plumbing drop out.
- **Conditional, mapped, indexed-access and generic instantiation:** `evaluate.rs` (775 lines) and most of `alias.rs` (844).
- **Dependency types:** `dependency_types.rs` (1,185 lines) loads dependency declarations ourselves. The checker resolves modules, `paths`, `exports` and `@types` already.
- **The silent-wrong families:** call signatures, alias wrappers, `& {}`, tuples and getters all come back correct from the checker. We map its answer, not parse the syntax ourselves.

**What stays ours:**
- **Oxc parse and extractor:** component detection, defaults, JSDoc, names and the fast first answer. That is the 50 ms structural path.
- **Output projections:** canonical JSON, TOON and the RDT shape for Storybook controls.
- **The structural resolver** as the fallback when no checker is available, but it can be smaller and less perfect.

**What not to take from tsrs:**
- Its parser and AST (36k lines of arena-based nodes, no stability promise, and no shared parse with the checker).
- `tsrs_pseudochecker` (it types initializer expressions, not annotations).
- The LSP, emit and incremental-project machinery. Our `WatchSession` is already a 2 ms path.

**Immediate wins, independent of the big decision:**
1. **Swap the oracle's checker to tsrs.** The weekly oracle runs the checker over five corpora. tsrs reproduced all 87 verdicts, and its own benchmark says it uses about half the memory and runs 2 to 3 times faster. That lowers the cost you flagged. The weekly workflow is the real consumer, so I'd want one confirming run there.
2. **Allow the tsrs binary in the supervisor** for the opt-in backend (a version allow-list line).

**Resulting shape.** Three layers: the oxc syntactic fast path, the checker (tsrs) as the type authority for what the fast path can't prove, and one shared projection model for the outputs. The `Ctx` and `DeclKey` ideas stay for the fast path, and the declaration table can shrink.

**Not verified:**
- The tsrs checker API beyond the 19 methods caliper calls today.
- Async framing with caliper's client.
- Latency of an in-process session against the 150 ms wait.
- How much of `dependency_types.rs` is really replaceable.
- Behaviour on large libraries such as Mantine and Chakra.

The tsrs spike answers most of those. Shall I start it, and do you want the oracle swap as a separate small change?

content.text:
I agree, and tsrs removes most of the reasons we kept it opt-in. I've updated my notes to record this as your direction. It is not yet a decision, because the earlier rule was that going default-on needs an ADR and oracle evidence.

**Why the earlier blockers are weaker now:**
- **Beta pin.** tsrs ports the same TypeScript commit as `typescript-beta` 7.1.0-beta.
- **Speed and memory.** It is typically 2 to 3 times faster and uses about half the memory, per its own benchmark.
- **Install friction.** Today users must install `typescript@7.1.0-beta` or point `tscPath` at one. `tsrs` ships prebuilt binaries on npm for seven platforms: macOS arm64 and x64, Linux x64 and arm64 (glibc and musl), and Windows x64. The `@tsrs/darwin-arm64` package is about 24 MB unpacked and `@tsrs/linux-x64-gnu` about 35 MB. Caliper could depend on it directly, so default-on needs no user setup.

**What default-on needs:**
1. **Per-surface defaults.**
   - **Storybook addon:** structural answer first, checker answer later and cached (ADR 0022), which keeps the first load imperceptible.
   - **CLI, TOON and agents:** wait for the checker, with a timeout, since correctness matters more than startup there.
2. **A fallback that never fails extraction.** On a missing binary, an unsupported platform, a crash or a timeout, the structural result is returned with one diagnostic. The lifecycle work in `crates/tsc-client` already does most of this.
3. **A distribution decision.** Add `tsrs` as an optional dependency of the npm packages. The package size grows by 24 to 35 MB per platform, so the cost should be weighed. Windows ARM64 is a listed tsrs gap, which gets the structural fallback.
4. **A version policy.** The pin follows tsrs releases, which come every two or three days, so we'd pin an exact version and bump deliberately.
5. **A new ADR** superseding the opt-in decision in ADR 0006 and 0007, plus evidence.

**Evidence without a corpus oracle run.** To respect your cost limit:
- The weekly workflow already runs the oracle every Monday, so switching its checker to tsrs gives the comparison for free.
- The spike measures time to first answer, resident memory and the async framing on one Chakra-sized project through caliper's real client.
- The 87-fixture parity run is already done.

**Effect on the structural work.** Treat the structural resolver as the fast path and fallback, not the authority. Keep the silent-wrong fixes (already in flight), and hold the deeper scoping branches and the evaluator threading.

Shall I start the spike now? It is one worker, with no oracle and no corpora, and it covers the in-process and binary modes, the framing check and the time to first answer. Its output feeds the ADR.

content.text:
The prototype shows the checker's structured API is enough for nearly everything `PropType` holds, and it beats our structural path on most of the sixteen components compared. I read the deep-dive worker's full report at `/tmp/claude-501/deepdive/FINAL.txt`. Everything below is its measurement unless I say otherwise, on tsrs 0.23.0 and macOS arm64. I haven't reproduced any of it.

**What it measured.**
- **Small project:** 16 components, the checker's first pass 51 ms, warm 14 to 16 ms, with 55 MB of memory. Caliper's structural path takes 20 ms and 56 MB.
- **Chakra `ButtonProps`** (1,854 files, 1,138 props):
  - The snapshot takes about 45 ms and the first answer 62 to 67 ms.
  - Converting every prop takes 365 to 383 ms, but that is the Node client's JSON over a pipe, which a Rust client should cut.
  - Memory is 128 MB.
  - Caliper takes 143 ms and 112 MB, and misses `export const ChakraDirect = Button`.
- **Quality:** the checker is better or equal on 14 of 16. It is better on conditional types (2 props we miss), tuples, getters, overloaded objects, enums, bigint and `string & {}`. It is worse on 2: a prop with an unresolved import comes back as `any`, and union members come back sorted instead of in declaration order.
- **Generics:** a virtual probe file (`Parameters<typeof Poly<'div'>>[0]`) gives 267 props in 7 ms. Caliper and a plain checker query give 2.
- **Watch mode:** a notified edit updates in 2.6 ms. An unnotified edit stays stale.

**Gaps and problems.**
- **Union order:** Storybook select options would reorder unless we re-apply the declaration order from our AST.
- **`PropType` can't hold:** tuple optional and rest elements, bigint, unique symbols, enum identity, template literals, overload sets, call signatures on objects, and a recursion marker. The structural path already gets some wrong: `[string, ...number[]]` becomes a double array, and a getter reads as a method.
- **React terminals** (`ReactNode`, `CssProperties`, `Ref`, `ElementType`) aren't checker concepts. We recognise them by declaring file.
- **Never key a cache on type ids,** because they change with query order.

**What could be deleted,** by line count only: about 9,400 of 25,300 lines if the structural fallback went entirely. With a thin fallback it is about 7,600.
- **Resolver:** 6,252 lines.
- **Dependency loading:** 1,828 lines (`dependency_types.rs` and `import_map.rs`).
- **Extractor:** about 1,300 lines.

The worker has not verified that specific helpers inside the shrinkable files are unused by the fallback. A fallback is still needed: tsrs has no win32-arm64 package, CI may be offline, and a crash needs a degraded answer.

**Risks, with the worker's evidence:**
- **Pre-1.0 churn:** eight npm betas since 0.20.0 between 2026-10-26 and 2026-11-07.
- **Memory in a long-lived dev server.** Measured growth was 148 MB over 150 Chakra edits. The relevant tsrs issues are:
  - #887: fixed on 2026-11-05.
  - #889 and #895 (session leaks): the fix merged the day before 0.23.0. I don't know which release contains it.
  - #920 and #646: still open.
  - The mitigation is to recycle the process at a size threshold.
- **Determinism across checker counts:** their docs warn about history-dependent diagnostics. A type-query test showed none, but only on a small project.
- **Open crash #860:** it is in the incremental build-info path, not the query path the prototype used.

**The proposed slice plan,** each slice gated without the oracle:
1. Add the new `PropType` variants (tuple flags, bigint, unique symbol, template and others), filled by the structural path.
2. Port `crates/semantic`'s converter to the full flag-based one, with a test that reversed query order gives identical bytes.
3. Recognise React terminals by declaring path.
4. Make the checker the default behind the existing structural-first window, with a CLI timeout of 10 s. The latency gate is a first answer within 150 ms on a warm Chakra project, measured with the Rust client.
5. Add an instantiation probe for generics.
6. Switch watch mode to snapshot updates.
7. Delete the structural resolver, keeping a thin fallback.
8. Flip the default and write the ADR.

The worker also drafted the ADR outline: "The checker is the type authority; oxc supplies syntax", with `--no-checker` as the opt-out and an exact version pin.

**My read.** This supports your direction. The strongest evidence is the generics probe and the 14 of 16 quality result. The things I would not claim yet are the Rust client's numbers, behaviour on large programs and other CPU counts, and long-running memory. Those gate slice 4, not slice 1.

**Effect on current work.**
- Hold the deeper structural scoping branches and the evaluator threading, as before.
- Slices 1 to 3 are safe to start after #379 and #385 merge. They also fix today's structural tuple and getter bugs.

Do you want me to open a trail for these slices, and start slice 1 once #379 lands?

**Gaps we can close ourselves:**
1. **`PropType` can't hold what the checker returns.** Add variants for tuple optional, rest and variadic elements, bigint, unique symbol, enum identity, template literals, overload sets, call signatures on objects, a recursion marker, and a typed `Truncated` (today the converter falls back to printing the checker's text as a name). Component-level index signatures need a place in `ParsedProp`. This is slice 1. It changes the canonical JSON contract (ADR 0017) and needs a schema version bump, so the projections have to follow.
2. **Union order.** The checker sorts members by flags and then value, not by declaration. For literal unions in our own files we re-apply the order from the oxc AST of the prop's type node. For a union declared in a dependency, we can parse that declaration file with oxc, from the declaration location the API returns, and read the members in order. This is medium effort, and it needs a test that reversed query order gives the same bytes.
3. **React terminals** (`ReactNode`, `CssProperties`, `Ref`, `ElementType`, `HTMLAttributes`). Recognise them by the declaring file path (`/@types/react/`). Small and mechanical.
4. **An unresolved import coming back as `any`** (the `TypeSampler.sx` case). This should become a `degradedBy` marker, not a silent `any`. In TypeScript an unresolved import yields an error type, but I have not verified how tsrs exposes it. That check comes first.
5. **Cache keys.** Never use type ids. Key by declaration location, file hashes and the checker version. The checker doesn't expose a per-component dependency closure, so start with coarse invalidation (any file in the program changed).
6. **Watch mode.** The unnotified edit that stays stale is our side: our watcher already sees edits, so it must notify the checker, including resolved dependency files.
7. **Conversion cost.** All 1,138 Chakra props took 365 to 383 ms through the Node client. We control the depth, the caps and the batching, and the Rust client should be lower.
8. **Descriptions, tags and parent.** The checker exposes `getJsDocTags` and `getDocumentationComment`. The prototype only spot-checked agreement with caliper, so a comparison is needed.

**Gaps we can only mitigate, because they live in tsrs:**
- **Memory growth in a long dev session.** The prototype measured +148 MB over 150 Chakra edits. Open tsrs issues #920 and #646 track leaks. Our mitigation is to recycle the process at a size threshold. The root fix is theirs.
- **No win32-arm64 package.** We keep a thin structural fallback, which we wanted anyway for crashes and offline CI.
- **Pre-1.0 churn,** with eight betas since 0.20.0. We pin an exact version and gate bumps on a deterministic test set.
- **History-dependent diagnostics across checker counts.** Their docs say this exists, but the type-query test on a small project showed none. Large programs are unmeasured.

**What is not verified:** the Rust client's timings (only the Node client was measured), large programs, memory past 150 edits, and the error-type behaviour in item 4.

**Recommended order:**
- Slice 1 (new variants, order, React terminals) first. It is independent of the checker decision, and it fixes bugs we have today in the structural path.
- Item 4 gets its verification and slice 2.
- After that comes the checker-default slice with the latency gate.

Slice 1 touches `types/` and the projections, so it waits for #379 and #385 to merge. Want me to open the trail now?

content.text:
Very little of our code belongs in tsrs. What we can give them is evidence and a few feature requests, and anything we post publicly needs your OK.

**Why little ports.** tsrs's job is to match TypeScript's checker exactly (its stated goal is 100% conformance). The things we do well are a different job:
- **Fast, program-free extraction:** the 50 ms structural run and the 2 ms incremental update work because they skip the checker.
- **Component logic:** detecting components, telling a helper from a component, destructuring defaults, JSDoc, framework wrappers and HTML attribute policy.
- **Output projections:** canonical JSON, TOON and the Storybook shape.

None of that is a checker concern, and a checker that did it would stop being a faithful port.

**What would help them, and us.** They accept issues but close pull requests, so these would be issues:
1. **Reproducible memory-growth numbers for long API sessions.** The deep-dive measured +54 MB over 1,500 small edits and +148 MB over 150 Chakra edits. Their open issues #920 and #646 are about exactly this. A concrete script on a public project is more useful than a description.
2. **Real-world benchmark projects.** Chakra and Mantine are not in their benchmark list. Our fixtures and the Chakra run could be added as a data point.
3. **Feature requests that would simplify us:**
   - A per-query dependency closure, so we can invalidate a cache precisely.
   - Stable type handles across snapshots (type ids change with query order today).
   - An option to return union members in declaration order.
   - A way to tell an explicit `any` from an error type caused by an unresolved import.
4. **Parity fixtures.** Our 87 one-prop fixtures all matched the Go checker. They are a small but cheap extra signal for them, though they are React-props specific.

**What I would not do.** I would not offer them the structural resolver. It approximates the checker, which is the opposite of their goal, and we're planning to shrink it.

**Caveats.**
- Their issues are triaged by a bot, and the two we found (#858, #871) had no maintainer reply, so I wouldn't expect fast answers.
- Item 3's requests depend on checking what the API already exposes. I haven't verified that none exists, and the unresolved-import question is the one I flagged earlier.

If you want, I can draft the memory-growth report and the feature requests as text for you to review, without posting. Posting is a public action under your account.

content.text:
Do the work first, and keep the oracle on the Go checker. That also corrects something I told you earlier.

**My earlier suggestion was wrong in one respect.** I said swapping the oracle's checker to tsrs was an immediate win because it is faster and lighter. If caliper makes tsrs the default type authority, an oracle that also runs on tsrs would mostly agree with caliper by construction. The oracle exists to be an independent arbiter. If both sides share one checker, a tsrs bug is invisible. So the oracle should keep using the Go checker (`typescript-beta`), and it becomes the check on tsrs itself.

**Why work first:**
- **The oracle is the instrument.** Changing the instrument while changing the thing it measures confounds the result. We would not know whether a number moved because of a fix or because of the swap.
- **The oracle isn't the gate for slice 1.** The new `PropType` variants, union order and React terminals can be gated by deterministic offline tests, as in the slice plan. No corpus run is involved.
- **Cost.** The weekly run is Monday CI minutes, not your agent tokens, and the savings from tsrs would be small.

**What I would do with the oracle, in order:**
1. **Merge #380** (the comparator fix), so `wrong` stops counting artifacts.
2. **Slice 1 and the construct suite** with deterministic gates. A committed one-prop fixture per construct, expected output captured from the Go checker, runs in seconds with no corpora.
3. **Later, fix the oracle's own blind spot:** its TypeScript program has no `paths`, so about 277 props are never judged. That change improves coverage.
4. **Add a small tsrs-against-Go parity check** on the fixtures, run whenever we bump the tsrs pin. It is the 87-row result made permanent, and it catches tsrs drift on a version bump.

**One exception.** If the weekly runs get expensive in CI, a tsrs-based run is a reasonable cost saver for the routine Monday record. In that case keep a periodic Go run, so the independence is not lost.

So: #380, then slice 1 with the offline suite, and no oracle change now. Want me to put the construct suite in as the first gate of the slice-1 trail?
